transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-29
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Markus Hale (Citrine CTO), Sofia Chen (Head of AI), Liam Ortiz (DevOps)

Auto Summary: (auto-generated, may be rough) Citrine has real-time scoring workload, wants reserved GPUs with strong tenant fencing, prewarm for sudden marketing spikes, and KMS integration. Interested in fallback to hosted if Dedicated saturates.

Topics: reserved GPUs sizing, warm pool / hotpool, eviction & preemption, KMS integration, P0 latency and cost tradeoffs

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00] Alex Monroe: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump into your workload. Uh I saw the calendar invite — Markus, Sofia, Liam, thanks for the time.
[00:12] Markus Hale: Yep thanks Alex. We, uh, appreciate it. We're trying to decide between Redwood Hosted for speed of onboarding versus Dedicated because we need isolation and predictable latency.
[00:22] Alex Monroe: Totally. That's exactly what we usually see. Priya's gonna walk through the operational pieces and then we'll get into burst patterns. Priya?
[00:28] Priya Shah: Hi all. Quick note, this call is intended to scope reserved capacity — how many GPUs, isolation topology, and how you want to handle spikes. I'll ask some questions as we go.
[00:36] Sofia Chen: Cool. High level -- we run a real-time recommender for e‑commerce, about 150ms 99p target for short queries, mostly sequence length ~64 tokens. Typical payloads are small JSONs, but bursts during promos can be 4-5x our baseline qps.
[00:52] Liam Ortiz: And for compliance: all inference logs need to stay in our VPC, keys in our KMS, and we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:02] Priya Shah: Understood. For KMS we do both managed and customer-managed keys, support HSM via integrations — it's the typical path. Quick Q: are you planning to run in our Dedicated offering within your VPC or private air-gapped?
[01:14] Markus Hale: We want the private deployment (VPC peering) for now. On‑prem might come later. The main ask is tenant fencing — we can't risk noisy neighbor impact.
[01:24] Alex Monroe: Right. We support multiple isolation patterns: node-level tenancy (dedicated nodes per customer), tenancy via VM/container isolation with strict cgroups, and soft multi-tenant with tenant quotas. For Citrine — sounds like node-level fencing is the recommended path.
[01:38] Sofia Chen: Can you explain the warm-pool model? We read about "hotpools" in the docs but not sure about eviction behavior when there's sustained surge.
[01:46] Priya Shah: Sure. We have a warm-pool (hotpool) that keeps a small number of prewarmed model instances in memory. On burst, we route to reserved nodes first, then hotpool, then fallback to either queued requests or to Hosted-compatible model variants — depending on policy. Eviction happens if reserve capacity is full and we've exceeded configured burst window.
[02:06] Liam Ortiz: Is the hotpool on the same physical host class as the reserved GPUs? We want predictable perf.
[02:10] Priya Shah: Typically yes, same GPU family. There are options to pin hotpool to dedicated hardware or place it in the shared warm pool for cost tradeoffs. Important to note: prewarmed kv-cache state isn't always transferable between quantized kernels, so we recommend same model binary for hotpool to avoid cold starts.
[02:28] Markus Hale: That "kv cash" thing — sorry, what was that?
[02:31] Priya Shah: K‑V cache. Sorry, the transcription assists sometimes turns it into 'kv cash' — it's the key/value cache used for autoregressive decoding to avoid recomputing prefixes.
[02:39] Sofia Chen: Makes sense. Our SLOs are strict. Cost is a concern; can we shape burst to degrade gracefully (e.g., lower max tokens or rerank fewer candidates) instead of full denial?
[02:51] Alex Monroe: Absolutely. We often recommend graceful degradation: shorter decode, reduced beam size, or switching to a smaller model during overload. That's part of the routing policy — latency-first or cost‑first policies.
[03:04] Markus Hale: What's your monitoring look like? We need per-tenant token-level billing and 99p latency traces.
[03:11] Priya Shah: Redwood Console provides token-level cost breakdowns, per-route dashboards, and tracing hooks. We'll also expose per-tenant dashboards in your private console. We can forward logs to your SIEM with an event stream for audit.
[03:23] Liam Ortiz: On network: we require egress restrictions — no outbound to public internet from the inference nodes except to our logging endpoints. Is that doable?
[03:31] Alex Monroe: Yes, for private we support VPC-restricted egress and customer-managed endpoints. We'll capture that in the security design.
[03:36] Sofia Chen: For sizing — we typically sustain 400 qps baseline with 2 large spikes a month up to 2,500 qps for 20–40 minutes. How would you recommend reserving?
[03:47] Priya Shah: Two approaches: reserve for baseline and rely on burst + hotpool + temporary capacity for spikes, or reserve for a conservative fraction of the burst and enable cross-customer bursts via pre-approved surge agreements. From your numbers I'd recommend reserving for baseline (400 qps) and sizing burst pool to handle a 3-4x delta. We'll model that in the benchmark.
[04:05] Markus Hale: What's the unit? GPUs per qps? This is where we get fuzzy.
[04:09] Priya Shah: It depends on model size and batch efficiency. For a mid‑sized LLaMA-class model at your seq length, we typically see 60–80 qps per A100-equivalent GPU with our batching. That number increases with batching and shorter latency budget. So for 400 qps baseline you might need 5–7 GPUs; for 2,500 qps you need more or rely on hotpool and burst nodes.
[04:29] Alex Monroe: We'll run an end-to-end benchmark with your payloads — Priya will send a load script. That will give precise GPUs needed.
[04:36] Sofia Chen: On security: SOC2 is required. Also we need proof of KMS flow: where keys live, who has access, and HSM support.
[04:44] Alex Monroe: We'll share SOC2 report and a KMS integration diagram. For HSM we support customer-managed HSM through partner integrations. We'll add the whitepaper link in the follow-up.
[04:54] Markus Hale: If we commit to a reserved pool, are there SLAs for preemption? For example, if the hardware fails or there's an AZ issue, what is the failover?
[05:04] Priya Shah: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and failover policies. We offer zone redundancy patterns, warm-standby nodes, and automatic failover to a fallback model/region. In the worst case Redwood Hosted can act as a spillover with graceful throttling, but we will define per-route fallback rules during rollout.
[05:20] Liam Ortiz: We need clarity on tenant quarantine — if a noisy tenant is detected, can we throttle/quarantine without impacting others?
[05:27] Priya Shah: Yes. We have tenant fencing and quota enforcement at both scheduler and runtime. We can isolate suspected noisy tenants to a quarantine pool and throttle their qps. There's also an eviction policy for runaway instances.
[05:36] Alex Monroe: Quick note — we also support isolation by GPU partitioning (MIG-like) for certain hardware, though it's not available across all GPU types. Good for higher density with some perf tradeoffs.
[05:47] Sofia Chen: Any concerns about model quantization and quality when we fallback to smaller variants during spikes? We can't degrade core quality.
[05:53] Priya Shah: That's a tradeoff we monitor with quality regressions tied to eval prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles that preserve quality. Also, we support A/B rollouts so you can test fallback variants before promoting them to safety nets.
[06:07] Markus Hale: Ok. Let's talk about contractual terms — commitment length, overage pricing, and burst accounting.
[06:12] Alex Monroe: We have monthly and annual reserved tiers. Burst can be charged as a separate add-on (metered) or included up to a certain cushion. We'll include both options in the pricing matrix.
[06:21] Liam Ortiz: One more technical — how do you handle KV cache warmup across requests if we use many short-lived containers?
[06:28] Priya Shah: If containers are short-lived we rely on hotpool and prefix caching at the router layer. For persistent sessions we keep KV in process to avoid recompute. There's always a tradeoff with ephemeral workloads.
[06:38] Sofia Chen: Any benchmark we can run quick? We can provide payloads today.
[06:42] Priya Shah: Yes. Priya will share the load script. We'll ask you to run it against a Redwood test endpoint; we'll also run our internal simulation. Expect a back-and-forth on batch settings and sequence length to calibrate.
[06:53] Alex Monroe: I'll send the Dedicated pricing matrix and the security pack. Also linking to the dedicated playbook — see: https://redwood.example.com/dedicated-playbook (internal link stub).
[07:03] Markus Hale: Perfect. One operational question: what is the minimum reserve?
[07:08] Priya Shah: Minimum reserve is 4 GPU-equivalents (billing unit) for Dedicated in most regions. We can discuss exceptions but that's the standard.
[07:15] Sofia Chen: Is there a dry-run/onboarding period so we can test performance before committing?
[07:19] Alex Monroe: We typically do a pilot: short-term reserved pool or a discount pilot with a benchmark. That's what we're proposing here.
[07:27] Markus Hale: OK, recapping: you will send pricing and security docs; Priya will send benchmark plan; we will provide traffic patterns and payloads; align on KMS diagram and schedule security deep-dive. Anything else?
[07:38] Alex Monroe: That's it from us. We'll add a proposed timeline in the follow-up email.
[07:43] Sofia Chen: Thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[07:46] Liam Ortiz: Thanks.
[07:48] Alex Monroe: Thanks all — next steps in email.
